title: How To Get Your Students To Listen To You
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the common frustration of giving a single direction and having a third of the class fail to follow it, escalating into repeated and eventually shouted instructions. His solution is the 'simple first' strategy, which trains students to listen to the sound of the teacher's voice by first giving a rapid sequence of simple, meaningless physical directions—stand up, sit down, stand behind your chair—before sliding in the actual important direction, such as taking out a textbook. He notes this works especially well for middle and high school teachers who lack time to build classroom management habits gradually, and lists supporting keys: stand in one place, give one direction at a time, never repeat yourself, pause between directions, use voice instruction without modeling, and keep volume low. Linsin claims the strategy takes only about a minute and needs to be used just a couple of times a week to remain effective.
points: The 'simple first' strategy trains students to listen by giving a rapid sequence of simple, meaningless physical directions before the real one.
Once students are reliably following the simple directions, slide in the actual important instruction, which they then follow precisely.
The technique is especially useful for middle and high school teachers who have limited time to build classroom management gradually.

quotes: You give a single direction to a quiet and seemingly attentive classroom, and then watch as a third of your students either don’t know what to do, or they do it incorrectly.
This strategy so effective, in fact, that you can use it with a group of students you’ve just met, and they’ll follow your directions like a champion drill team.
The way the strategy works is that you get your students listening to simple and physical directions first before giving more important directions.
If at this point all of your students are following along, slide in your important directions.
It also has staying power. Although it takes less than a minute, you won’t have to use it all the time. Just use it a couple of times a week or whenever you need it.
The “simple first” strategy is effective because it trains students to listen for the sound of your voice and to follow directions precisely and the first time they’re given.
